query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Annealing at 700 K relieves fabrication‐induced internal strain and induces short‐range atomic reordering in the as-deposited, amorphous Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 nanoribbons, which reduces local domain-pinning barriers and enhances collective ferromagnetic exchange. This change improves the magnetization and increases the isothermal magnetic entropy change while reducing hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, rare-earth-free Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 high-entropy alloy thin films and nanoribbon arrays that are amorphous or extremely fine/disordered with a single cubic-type short-range order and minimal surface roughness.
generation.intervention: Annealing the 1 µm-spaced nanoribbon arrays at 700 K in flowing Ar + 2% N2 at a rate of 10 K/min, ensuring the material remains in a metastable pre-crystallization state.
generation.conditions: Measurements should be performed under low applied fields (up to 50 kOe) across temperatures from ~40 K to 200 K, within the elastic regime (no external strain beyond inherent fabrication-induced stress), and verified by structural probes (TEM/SAED, AFM) to confirm the absence of bulk crystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range atomic reordering and relaxation of internal strain within the amorphous matrix that reduce the density of magnetic domain-pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: The annealing induces local atomic rearrangements that relax internal stresses, thereby reducing pinning barriers. This facilitates enhanced ferromagnetic alignment across magnetic clusters, which in turn increases the effective magnetic volume and spin-entropy variation. A reduced number of pinning sites lowers hysteresis during cyclic magnetic-field applications.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed 1 µm-spaced nanoribbon arrays are expected to show increased magnetization and a higher maximum conventional isothermal magnetic entropy change (−ΔSM) around 140 K, along with a reduction in hysteresis in M(H) loops. These improvements should occur without a shift in the principal blocking peak or alteration of in-plane isotropy.
generation.baseline: As-deposited, unannealed Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 nanoribbon arrays with a reported maximum −ΔSM ≈ 1.25 J kg−1 K−1 at ~140 K under 50 kOe.
generation.boundary: The enhanced magnetocaloric properties are expected only within the metastable, pre-crystallization regime at 700 K; annealing near 1000 K that leads to crystallization or studies beyond the elastic strain limit (>2%) are outside the scope of this hypothesis. The observation is specific to the non-equiatomic composition and the geometrical constraints (e.g., 1 µm spacing) of the nanoribbon arrays.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in magnetization and −ΔSM, as well as the degree of hysteresis reduction, may vary due to subtle differences in the initial fabrication-induced strain and short-range order. Additionally, overlapping effects from magnetoelastic anisotropy inherent to any applied strain could complicate the isolation of the annealing effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 nanoribbon arrays with 1 µm spacing under identical fabrication conditions. Subject one set to annealing at 700 K in Ar + 2% N2 (at 10 K/min) while keeping the other set as-deposited. Characterize both sets structurally (using TEM/SAED and AFM) to ensure the annealed samples remain amorphous and free of crystallization. Measure magnetic properties using SQUID magnetometry to obtain M(T) and M(H) curves and derive −ΔSM from isothermal magnetization curves across 40–200 K under low applied fields up to 50 kOe.
measurements: SQUID M(H) hysteresis loops at selected temperatures (e.g., 140 K)
TEM/SAED and AFM images to confirm structural state
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase (e.g., >10% improvement) in magnetization and maximum −ΔSM, or if there is no measurable reduction in hysteresis compared to the as-deposited samples, then the hypothesis that annealing-induced strain relaxation and short-range reordering govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis is rejected.
